mainEntity.name: What Should a Website Launch Handover Include?

acceptedAnswer.text: Seven things: the live URL and logins, what the client can edit themselves, what the retainer covers and excludes, how to request a change, where analytics live, backup and security details, and one named contact with a response time.

mainEntity.name: How Long Should a Client Handover Document Be?

acceptedAnswer.text: One page. Two at most. Anything longer gets skimmed once and never reopened, which puts you back where you started, answering the same questions by email.

mainEntity.name: Should I Charge for Small Post-Launch Changes?

acceptedAnswer.text: Log every one, then decide. Some are worth absorbing to keep a good client happy. The problem isn't giving work away, it's giving it away without knowing you did, which is how 57% of agencies lose four figures a month.

mainEntity.name: When Should the Handover Be Sent?

acceptedAnswer.text: The day the site goes live, in the same email as the launch announcement. Send it a week later and the client has already formed the habit of emailing you with questions.

mainEntity.name: Does a Client Portal Actually Reduce Emails?

acceptedAnswer.text: Only if the handover points at it. A portal nobody was told about is just another login. Name it in the pack, say what belongs there, and route the first two requests through it yourself.

HowTo.name: How to write a website launch handover pack
HowTo.description: The seven items to send a client on launch day so post-launch questions stop arriving by email.

step.name: The Live URL and Every Login
step.text: The domain plus the CMS login, and anything else registered in their name. Say plainly which accounts are theirs and which stay with you, because clients get quietly nervous about access and that nervousness surfaces as email six months later.

step.name: What They Can Safely Change Themselves
step.text: Text, opening hours, blog posts, prices. Name them specifically, because "you can edit the content" means nothing to someone who has never opened the editor.

step.name: What the Retainer Covers, and What It Doesn't
step.text: Both halves. Most packs list what's included and stop, which is exactly why you get asked about the rest. Write the exclusions plainly: new pages and design changes are quoted separately, as is anything needing a developer.

step.name: How to Request a Change
step.text: One channel, named. A ticket link, a portal, a form. Anything except "just email me", because "just email me" is how a request becomes a conversation and a conversation becomes free work.

step.name: Where the Numbers Live
step.text: Analytics access, plus the SEO tools if their plan includes them. Sitejet's XOVI integration gives them something concrete to look at, which beats a screenshot of traffic pasted into an email. It also opens the conversation about what comes next, whether that's ongoing SEO or scheduling their social posts through SocialBee.

step.name: Backups, SSL and Who to Call When Something Breaks
step.text: Say the backups exist, how often they run, and what happens when a site goes down. Clients almost never ask about this before launch. They ask at the worst possible moment.

step.name: One Named Contact and a Response Time
step.text: A person, not an inbox. "Ruth, within one working day" ends more anxiety than a support address ever will. It also stops them going around you to whoever answered fastest last time.
